messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ben was a man who lived by checklists and procedures, but for the last eight months, his own mind had become an unnavigable storm. It began on a Tuesday night, driving home from dinner with his then-wife. The sudden wash of red and blue lights in the rearview mirror was an annoyance, not a threat. But the stop that followed shattered his world. The officer, young and aggressive, ordered him out of the car with a voice that brooked no argument. An accusation of a DUI, which Ben knew to be false, escalated into him being pinned against the side of his own vehicle. He remembers the rough texture of the officer’s jacket against his ear, the smell of stale coffee, and the overwhelming physical closeness that felt like being suffocated. A wave of nausea, sharp and acidic, rose in his throat as he felt the utter loss of control. The incident ended as abruptly as it began with a passed breathalyzer and a curt dismissal, but the damage was done.

In the weeks that followed, the world became a landscape of hidden dangers. Ben, an airline pilot accustomed to managing immense pressure with calm authority, found himself flinching at the benign chime of a seatbelt sign or the sudden rumble of a catering truck on the tarmac. He began to feel a prickle of dread whenever a stranger walked towards him in the airport terminal, his body tensing for an attack that never came. He had come to believe that any unexpected event, any deviation from the plan, was a harbinger of disaster. A delay in pushback from the gate was no longer a logistical issue; in his mind, it became a sign that something was catastrophically wrong, a premonition of failure he had to watch for.

The memory of the event was not a passive recollection but an active assault. When it came, it brought with it the same gut-wrenching terror he had felt by the roadside, a full-body re-experiencing that felt more real and vivid than the cockpit instruments in front of him. At the same time, the memory felt so extreme, so out of place in the narrative of his life, that it was hard to believe it had actually happened. These memories would surface without warning, and in their wake, the world would reconfigure itself into a series of triggers. A co-pilot shifting in his seat would suddenly feel like an unbearable invasion of his space, the physical proximity igniting the same sense of being trapped and overpowered he’d felt when pinned against his car.

This constant state of threat became the lens through which he saw everything, and it relentlessly dragged the memory back to the forefront. The feeling of being on high alert, his heart hammering in his chest as a flight attendant approached the cockpit door, would make the memory of the officer’s face loom larger and more menacing in his mind. The present danger he perceived fed the past horror, making it feel immediate and ongoing. This heightened vigilance, in turn, made him exquisitely sensitive to his own body. The slightest hint of turbulence-induced nausea was no longer just a physical sensation; it was an echo of that initial wave of fear, a trigger that sent him spiraling back into a state of high alert, his hands gripping the yoke until his knuckles were white.

The cycles tightened over the months. Driving with anyone became impossible, straining his relationship with his crew. His marriage crumbled under the weight of his irritability and withdrawal. He began taking separate Ubers to the airport, unable to bear sharing a car with his colleagues. Ben came to therapy after a routine pre-flight walkaround. A ground crew member, meaning no harm, had clapped him on the shoulder to get his attention. The unexpected touch and closeness sent a jolt of pure panic through him, and he nearly stumbled backward off the tarmac. He realized then that his meticulously controlled world was shrinking to the point of collapse, and he was terrified of losing the one thing he had left: the sky.
